items.question: I ___ a shower when the doorbell rang.
explanations: ‘Had’ is past simple. The shower was already in progress when the doorbell rang, so use the past continuous.
Correct! The longer action (the shower) is past continuous; the short action that interrupts it (rang) is past simple.
‘Am having’ is present continuous, but the doorbell rang in the past.
‘Were’ goes with you/we/they. With ‘I’ use ‘was’.

items.question: While she ___ dinner, he was setting the table.
explanations: ‘Cooked’ is past simple. Two actions at the same time are both past continuous: was cooking … was setting.
‘Is cooking’ is present continuous, but this happened in the past.
‘Were’ goes with you/we/they. With ‘she’ use ‘was’.
Correct! Two actions happening at the same time both take the past continuous.

items.question: My parents ___ watching the news when I got home.
explanations: Correct! ‘My parents’ = they, so the past continuous uses ‘were’ + -ing.
‘Was’ goes with I/he/she/it. ‘My parents’ means ‘they’, so use ‘were’.
‘Did’ can’t go before an -ing form: we say ‘were watching’, not ‘did watching’.
‘Are’ is present, but ‘when I got home’ is in the past.

items.question: I ___ the answer, so I put my hand up.
explanations: ‘Know’ is a state verb, so it doesn’t take the continuous. Use ‘knew’.
‘Know’ is present, but ‘put my hand up’ happened in the past.
Correct! ‘Know’ is a state verb. State verbs don’t take the continuous, so we use the past simple: ‘knew’.
‘Have known’ is present perfect. This is a finished moment in the past: ‘knew’.

items.question: It ___ hard when we left, so we took umbrellas.
explanations: ‘Rained’ is past simple. The rain was already falling when we left, so use the past continuous.
‘Is raining’ is present, but ‘when we left’ is in the past.
‘Were’ goes with you/we/they. ‘It’ takes ‘was’.
Correct! The rain was already in progress when we left, and ‘we took umbrellas’ confirms it.

items.question: ___ they waiting for us when we arrived?
explanations: ‘Was’ goes with I/he/she/it. ‘They’ takes ‘were’.
Correct! Past continuous questions put ‘were’ first: Were they waiting…?
‘Did’ can’t go before an -ing form: Were they waiting…?
‘Are’ is present, but ‘when we arrived’ is in the past.

items.question: He broke his leg while he ___ skiing.
explanations: ‘Went’ is past simple. ‘While he …’ introduces a longer action in progress: ‘was going’ skiing.
‘Is going’ is present, but he broke his leg in the past.
Correct! ‘While’ introduces the longer action in progress, so we use the past continuous.
‘Were’ goes with you/we/they. With ‘he’ use ‘was’.

items.question: When the lights went out, we ___ a film.
explanations: Correct! The film was in progress; the lights going out is the short action that interrupted it.
‘Watched’ is past simple. The film was already in progress when the lights went out.
‘Watch’ is present, but the lights went out in the past.
‘Was’ goes with I/he/she/it. ‘We’ takes ‘were’.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I saw a snake while I walked in the forest.
I was seeing a snake while I was walking in the forest.
I saw a snake while I was walking in the forest.
I see a snake while I was walking in the forest.
explanations: The long action (walking) must be past continuous: ‘while I was walking’.
The short event (seeing the snake) is past simple: ‘I saw’, not ‘I was seeing’.
Correct! The short event is past simple (saw); the longer background action is past continuous (was walking).
‘See’ is present, but the sentence is about the past: ‘I saw’.

items.question: At six this morning, Lucy ___ for the train.
explanations: Correct! An action in progress at a specific past time (six this morning) takes was/were + -ing; ‘Lucy’ takes ‘was’.
‘Were’ goes with you/we/they. ‘Lucy’ takes ‘was’.
‘Is waiting’ is present, but ‘this morning’ at six o’clock is already past.
‘Waits’ is present simple, but we need the past continuous.

items.question: At eight o’clock last night, we ___ dinner. (eat)

common.why: An action in progress at a past time takes was/were + -ing.

items.question: You was sleeping when I called.
answers: You were sleeping when I called.
You were sleeping when I called
You were sleeping when I phoned

items.question: I was knowing the answer.
items.explanation: ‘Know’ is a state verb, so it doesn’t take the continuous: I knew the answer.
